Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are not the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.
So that brings me to the second group of people, who both
1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and
So that brings me to the second group of people, who both
2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research.
So that brings me to the second group of people, who both

This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and at the same time, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

Compound movement for the chest that also works the front and side deltoids and the triceps. Grip just outside shoulder width, lower the bar slowly to the chest, press up.
Dumbbells can be dropped to the side if a rep fails, but getting into position takes care: lift them to the knees, lean back, and kick them up to the shoulders.
Barbell or dumbbell; shifts work toward the upper chest and front deltoids. Dumbbells allow a deeper stretch at the bottom.

Lean forward somewhat to work the chest, front and side shoulders, and triceps. Add weight, such as a dumbbell held between the feet, once 10 to 15 bodyweight reps come easily. Huberman calls weighted dips an upper body squat.

Slight-incline dumbbell flies with a fixed bend in the elbows, cable flies, or a fly machine, which keeps resistance through the whole movement. Two to three work sets of 6 to 15 reps. Stand up before re-racking a weight rather than straining to set it down.
Lats, traps, and lower back. Two or three exercises, each with two or three work sets taken to failure.
Palms facing away. Think of driving the elbows back, as if elbowing someone behind you, and bring the chest toward the bar. Add weight once 10 to 12 good-form reps are possible.
For anyone not yet strong enough for pull-ups. Huberman prefers an underhand, close grip, pulling to just below the chest line.

Brace the core, lift the weight slightly to find the target muscle, row, and set the weight down rather than dropping it. Barbell and machine rows also work. Huberman shows no back isolation movements; compound pulls and rows with progressive overload are enough.
Deadlifts and rows work the traps. Shrugs are optional; people with rounded shoulders may want to skip them.
Back hyperextensions, 8 to 25 controlled reps, with a plate, dumbbell, or band for added load. Without a machine, hold a high countertop and lift the legs. Huberman does 100 reps a week.
A hanging progression that trains abs and grip together: knee raises to 90 degrees, then L-sits, then full pikes. The goal is three sets of five pikes.

Wide stance, toes slightly out, squat slowly with weight toward the heels. Press the elbows into the insides of the knees, then free one arm, point at the ceiling, and look up at the finger. Stretches the hips, thoracic spine, neck, and shoulder. Point at a corner of the room until full rotation comes.
Hip extension to stretch the hip flexors, which sitting, walking, stairs, and cycling all keep short. Standing, or in a kneeling lunge with the arm overhead.

Feet flat, knees bent, hands behind with fingers pointing out to the sides. A test of shoulder flexibility, not strength. Later progressions place the hands farther back and scoot the hips forward to stretch the biceps, held passively for 5 to 30 seconds.

Developed by Eric Goodman. Feet wider than shoulders and planted, push the hips back, lengthen the spine away from the tailbone, raise the arms, eyes forward, and exhale. Stretches the lower back; Huberman uses it as a physical and mental reset.
